title: Bay Ledger
statement: A loading dock has bays numbered 1 to bays in a row, all empty at first. Process the operations in order. ["set", bay, count] makes that bay hold exactly count boxes (replacing whatever it held). ["total", bay] reports how many boxes are in bays 1 to bay together. ["locate", k] numbers the boxes 1, 2, 3, ... starting from bay 1 and moving outward, and reports the bay that holds box number k, which is the smallest b such that bays 1 to b hold at least k boxes together; it reports -1 if the whole dock holds fewer than k boxes. Return the reports of the total and locate operations in order. A set operation produces no report.

examples.explanation: After the first two sets bay 3 holds 5 boxes and bay 6 holds 2. Bays 1 to 4 hold 5 boxes. Box 6 is the first box of bay 6 (bays 1 to 3 hold only 5), so locate 6 reports 6. Then bay 3 drops to 1 and bay 8 gets 9 boxes, so the running totals are 1 at bay 3, 3 at bay 6 and 12 at bay 8. Box 6 is now in bay 8, and box 14 does not exist, so the reports are 5, 6, 8, -1.
The dock is empty for the first two locates, so both report -1. After setting 3 boxes, total reports 3 and box 3 lives in bay 1.

hints.content: Every report depends on a running total over a prefix of the row. Which operations change a total, and how many prefix totals can one change disturb?
Rescanning up to 100,000 bays for each of 3,000 operations is hundreds of millions of steps. You need prefix totals that survive point updates.

A Fenwick (binary indexed) tree stores partial sums so that a point change and a prefix total each touch only O(log bays) cells. Feed it the difference between the new count and the old one when a bay is set.

For locate, prefix totals never decrease as the bay number grows, so the answer is found by binary search. Inside a Fenwick tree you can search in one descent: try jumps by decreasing powers of two and take a jump when its stored sum is still below the remaining target.
After the descent the position reached has a total below k, so the answer is the next bay, or -1 if you reached the last bay. Time is O(bays + operations * log bays).

testCases.explanation: Mixed sets, a prefix total and locates before and after an overwrite.
Setting a bay down to zero removes its boxes, so the dock is empty again.
Empty bays between stocked ones; locate at the boundary box of each stocked bay and past the last box.
A bay count that is not a power of two, with all boxes in the last two bays.
A random mix of 400 operations on 1,000 bays.
The largest dock: 400 stockings near the end of the row, then 2,600 totals and locates, each of which needs about 100,000 steps without a tree.
The largest input made only of sets with six-digit bay numbers; no reports are produced.
A dock whose size is exactly a power of two, with a random mix.
A random query-heavy mix on a dock one bay short of 100,000.

solutions.title: Scan the row for every report
solutions.intuition: Keep the counts in an array and add them up from bay 1 whenever a report is needed.
solutions.approach: set writes the array cell. total sums bays 1 to bay. locate adds bays from the front until the running sum reaches k.
solutions.pseudocode:
set: counts[bay] = count
total: sum counts[1..bay]
locate: running = 0; for bay in 1..bays: running += counts[bay]; if running >= k: return bay
        return -1
solutions.timeComplexity: O(1) per set, O(bays) per report: up to 3,000 * 100,000 = 300 million steps
commonMistakes: Adding a delta in set instead of replacing the count.
Returning the bay where the running sum first exceeds k instead of reaches it.
solutions.interviewExplanation: The array is the obvious model and is exactly right, but each report walks the row. With 100,000 bays and 3,000 operations the scan dominates, so a structure with logarithmic prefix sums is needed.

steps.title: Apply the sets
steps.content: Bay 3 holds 5 and bay 6 holds 2; total 4 sums bays 1 to 4 and finds 5.

steps.title: Scan for box 6
steps.content: The running sum is 5 after bay 3 and 7 after bay 6, so locate 6 stops at bay 6.

solutions.title: Block sums (square-root decomposition)
solutions.intuition: Group the bays into blocks of about sqrt(bays) and keep each block's sum, so a report skips whole blocks and scans only inside one.
solutions.approach: set updates the cell and its block sum. total adds full block sums and then the remaining single bays. locate skips blocks whose sum is below the remaining target, then scans the bays of the block that contains the target.
solutions.pseudocode:
size = ceil(sqrt(bays))
set: blockSum[(bay-1)/size] += count - counts[bay]; counts[bay] = count
total: sum whole blocks, then single bays
locate: skip blocks while blockSum < remaining, then scan inside the block
solutions.timeComplexity: O(1) per set and O(sqrt(bays)) per report: about 630 steps
commonMistakes: Off-by-one block indexes: bays are 1-based, so block = (bay - 1) / size.
Forgetting to subtract the old count from the block sum when a bay is overwritten.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Square-root decomposition trades a log factor for simplicity: about 632 steps per report instead of about 17 for a Fenwick tree, but the code has no bit tricks. With 3,000 operations both finish instantly, and it is a good fallback when you do not remember the tree.

steps.title: Blocks
steps.content: With 8 bays the block size is 3: blocks hold bays 1-3, 4-6 and 7-8.

steps.title: Locate
steps.content: Locate 6 on the first example skips block 1 (5 boxes) and finds the sixth box inside block 2 at bay 6.

solutions.title: Fenwick tree with a binary descent
solutions.intuition: A Fenwick tree makes both point changes and prefix totals logarithmic, and its layout lets a single descent find the first bay reaching a target.
solutions.approach: Keep counts in held and partial sums in tree. set adds (new - old) up the update chain. total adds down the query chain. locate starts at position 0, tries jumps of the largest power of two down to 1, takes a jump when the stored sum is below the remaining target (subtracting it), and finally answers position + 1 if that bay exists, else -1.
solutions.pseudocode:
set: delta = count - held[bay]; held[bay] = count; for i = bay; i <= bays; i += i & -i: tree[i] += delta
total: sum = 0; for i = bay; i > 0; i -= i & -i: sum += tree[i]
locate: pos = 0; for step = highest power of 2 <= bays down to 1:
  if pos + step <= bays and tree[pos + step] < remaining: pos += step; remaining -= tree[pos]
  answer pos + 1 if pos + 1 <= bays else -1
solutions.timeComplexity: O(bays + operations * log bays): about 17 steps per operation
commonMistakes: Adding the new count instead of the difference, double counting after an overwrite.
Starting the descent from a step larger than bays.
Using a strict test (tree <= remaining), which lands one bay too far when a prefix equals k exactly.
solutions.interviewExplanation: The Fenwick tree stores in cell i the sum of the last i & -i bays, so every prefix is a sum of at most 17 cells. Because totals are monotone in the bay number, the first bay reaching k can be found by building the largest prefix still below k one power of two at a time; the answer is the bay after it. Everything is logarithmic and the memory is one array.

steps.title: Stock the dock
steps.content: set 3 = 5 adds 5 to cells 3 and 4 and 8; set 6 = 2 adds 2 to cells 6 and 8.

steps.title: Descend
steps.content: For locate 6 the jump of 8 has stored sum 7, which is not below 6, so it is rejected. The jump of 4 has sum 5, below 6, so it is taken and the remaining target becomes 1. The jump of 2 reaches cell 6 with sum 2, not below 1, so it is rejected; the jump of 1 reaches cell 5 with sum 0, below 1, so it is taken. The position is 5 and the answer is bay 6.
